messages.content: I want to design distributed Adam state management that supports elastic resharding and crash recovery without mixing optimizer steps or duplicating updates. What are the core requirements?

The correctness requirement is that, after any single worker crash during resharding, the recovered parameters and moments match uninterrupted deterministic execution. That rules out a recovered state assembled from different optimizer steps, and it rules out applying an update twice. The performance requirement is to limit failure-free step-time overhead to 10% versus static sharding with identical hardware and workloads.
What does it mean to avoid mixing optimizer steps?

The parameters and Adam moments recovered for a given point in execution must be consistent with that point. For example, taking a parameter value associated with one step and moments associated with another would not satisfy the requirement merely because each value was individually available. Resharding must not make a combination of states from different steps appear to be one valid recovered state.
Is avoiding duplicate updates a separate concern?

Yes. Even if the state appears internally consistent, applying the same optimizer update more than once could make the parameters or moments diverge from uninterrupted deterministic execution. The design needs to preserve the intended sequence of updates through resharding and recovery, without counting an update twice.
Why does resharding matter to that sequence?

Elastic resharding changes how distributed state is assigned while optimization may also be progressing. The design therefore has to keep the state associated with an optimizer step unambiguous across that change. The requirement does not prescribe how to coordinate those activities; it specifies the result they must preserve, including when a worker crashes during resharding.
Does the recovery requirement cover only parameters?

No. It explicitly covers both parameters and moments. Recovering the expected parameters while the moments correspond to a different execution state would not meet it. The comparison is to the parameters and moments from uninterrupted deterministic execution.
Suppose recovery produces a state from which training can continue. Is that enough?

Not by itself. Being able to continue does not establish that the recovered parameters and moments match the uninterrupted deterministic reference. That match is the stated correctness test after any single worker crash during resharding.
How broad is the crash condition?

It says any single worker crash during resharding. The word “any” matters: the design cannot rely on the crash occurring only at a convenient point in the resharding process. The requirement does not, however, state a guarantee for multiple worker crashes.
Does “uninterrupted deterministic execution” mean we can compare against whichever recovered result looks plausible?

No. It supplies a reference: what the parameters and moments would be under uninterrupted deterministic execution. Recovery must match that reference rather than merely yield a plausible optimizer state. The node does not specify a separate numerical tolerance or a particular validation procedure.
How should I interpret the 10% figure?

It is a limit on failure-free step-time overhead relative to static sharding, using identical hardware and workloads for the comparison. In proportional terms, the design’s failure-free step time must be no more than 1.10 times the static-sharding step time under that comparison.
Does that 10% also set a limit on how long recovery takes after a crash?

The stated limit is specifically for failure-free step-time overhead. It does not separately give a recovery-time limit. Crash recovery still has to meet the correctness requirement for parameters and moments.
So should correctness be judged only when resharding finishes normally?

No. Normal completion alone would miss the explicit failure case. The design has to support elastic resharding without mixing steps or duplicating updates, and after any single worker crash during resharding it has to recover parameters and moments matching uninterrupted deterministic execution.
Can we choose a particular state-transfer or recovery method from these requirements alone?

These requirements define what a method must achieve, but they do not choose a particular method. Any proposed approach would need to account for step consistency, non-duplication of updates, the specified crash condition, and the 10% failure-free step-time comparison without treating those as already demonstrated results.
What is a concise way to keep the two tests distinct when discussing a design?

Ask two separate questions: after any single worker crash during resharding, do the recovered parameters and moments match uninterrupted deterministic execution without mixed steps or duplicate updates? And, with identical hardware and workloads, is failure-free step-time overhead no more than 10% versus static sharding? Passing one test does not by itself establish the other.
What approach would you propose for the distributed Adam state?

I’d propose epoch-fenced Adam shards, pipelined buddy-replicated step deltas, atomic commit markers, and copy-on-write resharding with idempotent replay. Together, those are meant to keep optimizer steps distinct as ownership changes and to make recovery possible without applying an update twice. It is a proposed design, not yet a demonstration that the crash-recovery or overhead requirements are met.
What is an epoch-fenced Adam shard?

An epoch is a way to distinguish one assignment of shard responsibility from another. Fencing means that work associated with an earlier assignment cannot silently act as though it belongs to the current one. In this proposal, that distinction is intended to prevent a resharding transition from making operations under different ownership assignments indistinguishable.
Is the epoch the same thing as an optimizer step?

No. They distinguish different dimensions: an optimizer step identifies progress through updates, while an epoch distinguishes a shard-assignment context. Both matter here because a step must not be mixed with another step, and an operation from an outdated assignment must not be mistaken for an operation under the current assignment.
What would the buddy replicate?

The proposal says to buddy-replicate step deltas: changes associated with optimizer steps, rather than describing the buddy simply as a second shard owner. For the recovery requirement, the available state and those deltas would have to suffice to recover both parameters and moments. The proposal does not yet specify their exact representation.
Why call the replication pipelined?

“Pipelined” suggests overlapping replication work with other step processing rather than treating every transfer as a wholly separate period of work. That is relevant to the 10% failure-free step-time overhead limit, but pipelining alone does not show that the limit will be met. It also cannot justify treating a partially replicated step as a fully committed one.
Then what do atomic commit markers add?

They provide an unambiguous committed-versus-not-committed distinction for a logical step. The purpose is to avoid interpreting a partial transition as a completed update, particularly if a crash occurs during resharding. The proposal does not specify the marker’s representation or an exact commit sequence.
Could the presence of a step delta alone serve as proof that the step committed?

Not under the distinction this proposal is trying to make. A delta being available and a step being committed are different questions. Atomic commit markers are proposed so recovery need not infer commitment solely from the presence of transferred or replicated data.
How does copy-on-write fit with resharding?

Copy-on-write resharding suggests preparing a changed shard layout without immediately overwriting the state needed to interpret the existing one. Conceptually, that gives the transition a way to preserve a coherent state while ownership changes. It does not, by itself, settle which optimizer steps are committed; that is why the proposal also includes fencing and commit markers.
Does that mean two layouts are both allowed to apply updates?

No. Preserving state while preparing a new layout should not be read as permission to apply the same logical update through both layouts. Epoch fencing and the commitment distinction are intended to keep an old assignment from competing with the new one. The exact handoff procedure remains unspecified in the proposal.
What does idempotent replay do after a crash?

It means replaying a logical update must not change the outcome merely because that update was encountered again during recovery. A committed update must not be applied twice, and replay must respect the distinction between committed and uncommitted work. The proposal names that property without prescribing a particular replay record or duplicate-detection mechanism.
Is idempotent replay enough on its own to prevent mixed steps?

No. Idempotence addresses duplicate application of the same logical update. Avoiding mixed steps also requires a coherent account of which step each recovered parameter and moment belongs to. The epoch fences, step deltas, and atomic commit markers are proposed to help maintain those distinctions across resharding.
Walk me through the intended recovery idea without assuming a specific protocol.

At a conceptual level, recovery would identify the relevant shard-assignment epoch and which optimizer steps are committed, then use the available state and buddy-replicated deltas as needed to produce that committed state. Replay would have to be idempotent so encountering an update again would not duplicate it. The result would still need to be checked against the stated requirement: after any single worker crash during resharding, both parameters and moments must match uninterrupted deterministic execution. This outline does not assert that the proposed components already guarantee that outcome.
Why emphasize both parameters and moments again?

Because an Adam step affects optimizer state as well as parameters. A recovery scheme that resolves which parameter update committed but leaves moments from another step would still mix optimizer steps. The proposed deltas, commitment distinction, and replay would have to preserve a consistent recovered state for both.
If a worker crashes halfway through copying a shard, does copy-on-write automatically solve recovery?

Not automatically. Copy-on-write is intended to avoid depending on an overwritten or partially changed view, but recovery also needs to determine which steps committed and avoid duplicate application. A crash partway through resharding is within the stated single-worker-crash condition; meeting the required result in that case has to be established for the combined design, not assumed from one component.
Where might the performance requirement constrain this proposal?

Fencing, replication, commit tracking, and copy-on-write can all involve work on the failure-free path, so their combined effect matters. Pipelining is part of the proposal, but whether the overall step-time overhead stays within 10% versus static sharding must be evaluated with identical hardware and workloads. The proposal supplies no overhead measurement.
So the intended division of labor is fencing for assignment changes, markers for committed steps, and replay for duplicate updates?

That is a useful conceptual reading, with buddy-replicated step deltas supplying recovery information and copy-on-write supporting the resharding transition. The mechanisms must work together: distinguishing assignments is not the same as distinguishing committed steps, and neither alone prevents a repeated replay from duplicating an update.
What should we avoid claiming about this design at this point?

We should not claim that it already recovers exactly after any single worker crash during resharding, or that it already meets the 10% failure-free overhead limit. We can state the proposed components and their intended roles. Their precise coordination and whether they satisfy both requirements remain to be established.
How should an epoch-fenced shard distinguish committed step deltas from in-flight copies after its owner crashes mid-reshard?

It needs to distinguish two facts that a crash can make easy to confuse: whether a step delta was committed, and whether some state was copied toward a new shard assignment. In the proposed design, an atomic commit marker is the intended evidence of commitment; the presence of copied data alone is not. The epoch fence identifies the shard-assignment context in which an operation belongs, but an epoch by itself does not prove that a particular optimizer step committed.
So a copy could be present without its step being committed?

Yes. During resharding, an in-flight copy might contain data associated with work whose committed status has not been established. Its presence shows that copying occurred, not that the corresponding step crossed the commit boundary. Recovery should not turn that physical observation into a claim that the step completed.
What if the copied data looks complete?

Looking complete is still different from having an unambiguous commitment decision. The question is not only whether all the expected data appears to be there; it is whether recovery can identify which optimizer steps are committed and assemble parameters and moments from a consistent point. The proposed atomic commit markers are meant to make that distinction explicit.
What exactly does the epoch fence contribute after the owner has crashed?

It keeps operations associated with different shard assignments distinguishable. After an owner crash mid-reshard, recovery must not mistake an operation belonging to the former assignment for an authorized operation under the changed assignment. Fencing addresses that ownership ambiguity; the commit marker addresses the separate question of whether a step completed.
Could recovery simply trust everything in the new shard layout?

Not solely because it is in the new layout. Copy-on-write resharding can leave copied state available while a transition is still in progress. Recovery needs to interpret that state using the applicable epoch and step-commit information, rather than treating placement in a destination as proof of commitment.
And should it trust everything left in the old layout instead?

Location in the old layout is not sufficient proof either. The old and new copies may tell recovery what data is available, but neither location alone answers which step deltas were committed. The aim is to recover one coherent sequence of committed optimizer steps, not choose a layout and assume every value in it has the same status.
How do the buddy-replicated deltas help with that distinction?

They are proposed as available step-delta information if the owner crashes. But replication of a delta and commitment of its step are distinct facts. A buddy-held delta can be relevant to recovery without being treated as automatically committed merely because a copy exists.
If the same delta can be found in both a copied shard and the buddy's state, what prevents two applications?

That is the role intended for idempotent replay in conjunction with the commitment distinction. Recovery must recognize a logical step as one update, even if information about it is encountered in more than one place. It cannot treat two copies of a delta as two optimizer steps. The proposal does not yet specify the exact way replay recognizes that duplication.
Does an atomic marker mean that the shard copy itself has to be atomic?

Not necessarily. The proposed marker concerns the decision that a logical step is committed. Copy-on-write resharding concerns how state remains interpretable while it is copied. The key distinction is that an incomplete or in-flight copy must not, by itself, create an apparent committed step; the proposal does not prescribe an atomic copy operation.
What is the dangerous case if we fail to keep those concepts separate?

Recovery could accept a parameter value from a copied state while taking moments from a different step, or it could replay a delta that was already applied. Either outcome would break the requirement to recover parameters and moments matching uninterrupted deterministic execution after any single worker crash during resharding.
Could the epoch number itself stand in for a step-commit marker?

Not without conflating assignment and update progress. An epoch says which shard-assignment context an operation belongs to; a step-commit marker says whether a particular optimizer step is committed. The proposal includes both because a reshard can change ownership without those two questions becoming the same question.
How would you state the recovery rule at a high level, without choosing a specific protocol?

Interpret available copies and buddy-replicated deltas in their epoch context, determine committed steps using an unambiguous commitment distinction rather than copy presence, and replay without applying any logical update twice. The recovered parameters and moments must then correspond to the same committed progression. That is a design criterion, not a claim that the currently proposed components have already been proved sufficient.
What remains unresolved in the question?

The proposal does not specify how commit markers and copied or replicated deltas are coordinated when the owner crashes at a particular point mid-reshard. That coordination is what would have to make commitment unambiguous despite an in-flight copy, while preserving epoch fencing and idempotent replay. The question identifies that gap without supplying a completed crash-recovery protocol.
Could replicated (epoch, step) commit watermarks and watermark-tagged copies distinguish committed deltas from in-flight copies after an owner crashes mid-reshard?

That is a plausible hypothesis. A replicated (epoch, step) commit watermark would identify committed progress in a particular shard-assignment epoch, while a watermark tag on a copy would identify the progress that copy represents. A replacement could then use the commitment information to discard uncommitted deltas and replay committed updates once. Whether the combination actually guarantees that behavior depends on details the hypothesis does not specify.
Why put both an epoch and a step in the watermark?

They identify different things. The epoch distinguishes the shard-assignment context; the step distinguishes optimizer progress within that context. Together, they would let a replacement interpret a copied state and its deltas without treating a step associated with one assignment as though it belonged to another.
What would a watermark tag on a copy tell the replacement?

It would state the committed progress the copy is meant to represent, in (epoch, step) terms. That makes the copy more informative than an unlabelled collection of parameters and moments: the replacement can ask which committed updates are already reflected there and which, if any, need replay. The tag must actually correspond to the copy’s contents for that interpretation to be sound; the hypothesis does not specify how to ensure that correspondence.
So the tag does not make the copy trustworthy just by existing?

Right. A tag is useful only if the copy and its tag describe a coherent state. If the tag claimed one step while the parameters and moments embodied another, the replacement could still mix steps. The hypothesis proposes watermark-tagged copies, but it does not itself establish the rule that makes each tag accurate.
What does replicating the commit watermark add?

It is meant to leave commitment information available when the shard owner crashes. A replacement would not have to infer committed progress solely from whatever data happened to be copied or from the presence of a delta. Replication helps preserve the distinction between ‘this information exists’ and ‘this optimizer step committed.’
If the replacement sees a delta beyond the committed watermark, what does the hypothesis suggest?

It suggests treating that delta as uncommitted and discarding it rather than incorporating it into recovered parameters or moments. Seeing the delta on a buddy or in an in-flight copy would not, by itself, change its status. That interpretation assumes the watermark is an authoritative and coherent indication of commitment, which still needs to be arranged by the design.
And what about an update marked committed but missing from the copy?

The hypothesis suggests replaying committed updates that the copy does not yet reflect, using the copy’s watermark tag to identify its starting point. Replay must apply each logical update once, even if information about the same update is present in multiple places. The hypothesis does not specify how a replacement obtains every needed delta or verifies that the necessary information is available after the crash.
Could it instead replay every delta it finds, then rely on idempotence?

Not without first respecting commitment. Idempotence prevents a committed logical update from having an extra effect when encountered again; it does not turn an uncommitted delta into an update that should be applied. The proposed watermark separates the eligibility question from the duplicate-application question.
What does ‘replay committed updates once’ mean when the copy might already include some of them?

It means counting each committed logical update exactly once in the recovered state. A committed update already reflected in the tagged copy should not be added again; one that is committed but not reflected there would need to be incorporated. The tag is intended to make that distinction possible, provided it accurately identifies the copy’s contents.
Would the watermark need to be considered separately from the location of the copy?

Yes. A copy’s location during resharding says where data was transferred, not how far committed optimizer execution progressed. The proposed tag records that progress explicitly, and the replicated commit watermark supplies commitment information independently of whether a copy is old, new, or still in flight.
What if two visible copies carry different watermark tags?

Different tags would indicate that the copies purport to represent different points of committed progress. The replacement should not combine their parameters and moments as if they represented one step. The hypothesis points toward interpreting each copy by its own tag and the replicated commitment information, but it does not specify a selection rule for that situation.
Does a watermark tagged with a later step automatically make that copy preferable?

Not automatically. A later tag is useful only if it accurately describes a coherent copy and is consistent with committed progress. The hypothesis does not state that every visible copy is complete or that a higher tag alone establishes which copy recovery should use.
How would this relate to epoch fencing?

The epoch component lets a replacement interpret commitment and copies in their assignment context, while fencing is meant to prevent operations from an outdated assignment from being accepted as current ones. A watermark is not a substitute for that fence: identifying where a step belongs and preventing an old owner’s work from being accepted are related but distinct needs.
Can a replacement simply use the highest replicated watermark it can see?

That would require more justification than the hypothesis supplies. The replicated watermarks need a well-defined meaning after a crash; mere visibility of a value does not by itself establish that copies, deltas, and commitment agree with it. The hypothesis is that such watermarks can support correct recovery, not a complete rule for choosing among visible values.
Where is the sharpest consistency issue in this idea?

The watermark, the copy’s tag, and the copy’s actual parameters and moments must describe compatible committed progress. If any of those disagree, discarding deltas beyond the watermark or replaying deltas after the tag could produce the wrong state. The hypothesis leaves open how that agreement is maintained when a crash interrupts resharding.
Does replicating the watermark mean the replicated step deltas are committed too?

No. The presence of a replicated delta still says that delta is available, not that its step committed. The proposed replicated (epoch, step) commit watermark is what would distinguish committed progress from deltas that were copied or replicated while still in flight.
What would count as evidence for this hypothesis rather than just a plausible explanation?

A design would need to show that after any single worker crash during resharding, a replacement can interpret the replicated commitment information and tagged copies unambiguously, discard uncommitted deltas, and incorporate each committed update once. The resulting parameters and moments would have to match uninterrupted deterministic execution. Those properties are what the hypothesis aims to enable; they have not been demonstrated here.
And does the hypothesis say anything definite about the 10% failure-free step-time overhead limit?

No. Replicating commit watermarks and tagging copies may introduce work, but the hypothesis gives no measurement or analysis showing whether failure-free step-time overhead stays within 10% versus static sharding with identical hardware and workloads. Its specific claim is about how replacements might distinguish committed work and replay it once.
What should we do next to resolve how an epoch-fenced shard distinguishes committed step deltas from in-flight copies after its owner crashes mid-reshard?

The plan is to specify the ordering between commit watermarks and copies, implement fenced replay, then inject crashes throughout resharding and compare recovered states and step latency. That moves from defining what recovery may trust, to implementing how it replays updates, to testing correctness and performance. These are planned activities, not completed results.
What needs to be specified about watermark and copy ordering?

The specification needs to make clear how a watermark relates to the state represented by a copy. After a crash, a replacement must be able to tell which committed steps the copy reflects and which deltas, if any, remain to be replayed. Merely having a watermark and a copy is not enough if their relationship is ambiguous.
Are we choosing an exact ordering rule now?

No. Specifying that rule is the first part of the plan. We should not assume a particular sequence of copying, tagging, and committing before defining how those events are meant to be interpreted when a crash interrupts them.
Why put that specification before implementing replay?

Fenced replay needs a clear distinction between a committed update that a copy already reflects, a committed update it does not yet reflect, and an uncommitted delta. The watermark-and-copy ordering is intended to establish that distinction. Without it, an implementation could replay the wrong set of deltas even if it recognizes epochs correctly.
What should implementing fenced replay accomplish?

It should make replay respect the shard-assignment epoch and the committed-step boundary, so that recovery does not accept an update under the wrong assignment or apply a logical update twice. Implementation is a planned step; whether it accomplishes those properties has to be checked rather than assumed.
Does fencing itself tell replay which deltas are committed?

No. Fencing distinguishes the assignment context in which an operation belongs. Commitment is a separate question addressed by the watermark-and-copy relationship. The planned replay needs both distinctions to avoid treating an in-flight copy as proof of a committed step.
What does injecting crashes throughout resharding add?

It exercises recovery when the owner crashes at different points in the resharding transition, rather than only when copying has finished neatly. That is important because the correctness requirement covers any single worker crash during resharding. The plan does not yet specify the injection procedure or report its results.
Should those crash tests check only that recovery completes?

No. Completion alone would not show that recovery preserved Adam state. The planned state comparison should check recovered parameters and moments against uninterrupted deterministic execution, including whether optimizer steps were mixed or an update was duplicated.
Why compare moments separately from parameters?

Both are part of the required recovered state. Parameters that match the deterministic reference would not be enough if the moments came from a different optimizer step. Comparing both helps assess whether the watermark ordering and fenced replay preserved one coherent progression.
If a crash test finds a delta in a copy, can the test count that as a committed update?

Not just because the delta is present. The ordering specification is supposed to establish how a copy’s contents and the commitment watermark relate. The test should judge the recovered state against uninterrupted deterministic execution, rather than infer commitment from a copied delta’s mere presence.
What exactly are we comparing for performance?

Step latency is the planned performance comparison. For the stated overhead requirement, the relevant comparison is failure-free step time versus static sharding with identical hardware and workloads, with overhead limited to 10%. Crash-injection runs address recovery correctness; they do not, by themselves, establish failure-free step-time overhead.
Is measuring step latency before implementing fenced replay enough?

It would not evaluate the planned design as a whole. The sequence here is to specify the ordering, implement fenced replay, and then compare step latency along with states. The 10% limit concerns the failure-free behavior of the resulting approach, not an isolated component viewed apart from it.
Could correct recovered states make the latency comparison unnecessary?

No. State agreement addresses the crash-recovery requirement, while failure-free step-time overhead is a separate requirement. The plan includes both state and latency comparisons so success on one is not mistaken for evidence of success on the other.
And if step latency is within 10%, does that tell us recovery is correct?

No. A low failure-free overhead does not show what happens after a worker crashes mid-reshard. The crash injections and state comparisons are needed to assess whether recovered parameters and moments match uninterrupted deterministic execution.
Does this plan establish that the watermark approach works?

Not yet. It sets out how to make the watermark-and-copy relationship precise, implement replay under epoch fencing, and test the resulting behavior. Until those steps are carried out and the states and step latency are compared, neither the recovery guarantee nor the overhead limit has been demonstrated.
Can you give me the plan in one sentence without implying the tests have happened?

Specify watermark and copy ordering, implement fenced replay, then inject single-worker crashes throughout resharding and compare recovered parameters and moments with uninterrupted deterministic execution, alongside failure-free step latency against static sharding on identical hardware and workloads.
What concrete crash-injection activity should we run?

Run 10,000 seeded single-worker crash injections at copy/commit boundaries. For each recovered run, compare parameters and moments bitwise, and compare applied-step IDs, against uninterrupted Adam. This describes the activity and its checks; it does not report an outcome.
Why specify 10,000 injections rather than just saying we will test crashes?

It makes the planned extent of the activity explicit: 10,000 seeded injections, each involving a single worker crash. That is a test count, not a claim that every possible crash timing has been covered or that recovery has succeeded.
What does ‘seeded’ add here?

Seeding makes the injections reproducible in principle. That matters when comparing a recovered run with uninterrupted Adam: the comparison should not be confused by unrelated variation between executions. The activity does not specify the seeds or how they are chosen.
Are these 10,000 workers crashing together?

No. ‘10,000 seeded single-worker crash injections’ means 10,000 injections of a single-worker crash, not one injection in which 10,000 workers crash. The activity targets the single-worker failure condition.
Why concentrate the injections at copy/commit boundaries?

Those are the boundaries where copied state and committed optimizer progress must be distinguished. A crash there can expose whether recovery treats an in-flight copy as committed work or overlooks an update that did commit. The activity identifies those boundaries as injection targets without specifying an exact list of crash points.
Does ‘at copy/commit boundaries’ mean we can assume copying and committing happen atomically together?

No. The wording calls out the boundary between copying and commitment as something to test, not an assumption that the two are one atomic action. The recovered state still has to be compared with uninterrupted Adam rather than judged from the mere presence of copied data.
What exactly gets compared with uninterrupted Adam?

The recovered parameters, the recovered moments, and the applied-step IDs. The parameters and moments receive a bitwise comparison. The applied-step IDs provide a separate check of which optimizer steps were applied, so an apparently plausible state is not the only observation.
Why require a bitwise comparison for parameters and moments?

It sets a strict equality check against uninterrupted Adam, rather than accepting values because they are numerically close. Checking both parameters and moments matters because they must represent the same intended optimizer progression after recovery.
Could the parameters match bitwise while the test still fails?

Yes. The specified comparison includes moments and applied-step IDs as well. Matching parameters alone would not establish that the full Adam state and the set of applied steps agree with uninterrupted Adam.
What do the applied-step IDs reveal that a state comparison might not make obvious?

They make the update history being counted visible to the comparison. If recovery omitted an applied step or counted one twice, the IDs could expose that discrepancy directly. Their inclusion does not replace the bitwise checks on parameters and moments; all three are part of the stated activity.
Should we count a delta as applied because it was copied before the crash?

No. A copy’s presence does not itself establish that the delta’s optimizer step was applied. The applied-step IDs and recovered state are to be compared against uninterrupted Adam, so the test must not define success by assuming an in-flight copy was a committed update.
What about a committed step that recovery has to replay?

The comparison should reflect that step once in the recovered state and applied-step IDs, as it would in uninterrupted Adam. Whether replay actually accomplishes that is what the activity is intended to examine; it is not an observed result.
If all 10,000 comparisons matched, what would that say?

It would be evidence that recovery produced matching parameters, moments, and applied-step IDs for the seeded single-worker crashes injected at the tested copy/commit boundaries. It would not, by the test count alone, prove behavior at every possible crash point.
And if one comparison differed?

Then that injected run would not meet the specified comparison with uninterrupted Adam. Looking at which of the parameters, moments, or applied-step IDs differed would help identify the observed discrepancy, without assuming its cause from the mismatch alone.
Is this activity also a step-latency measurement?
No. This activity specifies crash injections and comparisons of bitwise parameters, moments, and applied-step IDs. It does not specify measuring step latency or provide a performance result.
Can you restate the test instruction precisely, without presenting it as completed?

Run 10,000 seeded single-worker crash injections at copy/commit boundaries, then compare recovered parameters and moments bitwise and compare applied-step IDs against uninterrupted Adam. Record the comparisons as test outcomes rather than assuming they match.
What did the seeded crash comparisons show?
Across 10,000 seeded crashes, the recovered parameters and moments matched the uninterrupted Adam baseline bitwise. The applied-step logs showed zero omissions and zero duplicates.
Does ‘matched bitwise’ apply to both parts of the recovered Adam state?
Yes. The reported bitwise match covers both parameters and moments. It is not a statement about parameters alone.
And what was checked in the applied-step logs?

The reported log result is zero omitted steps and zero duplicated steps across those crashes. That is a distinct observation from the bitwise state comparison: it addresses which updates were counted, while the state comparison addresses the resulting parameters and moments.
Could you put the two observations together without overstating them?

For the 10,000 seeded crash cases, recovery produced parameters and moments bitwise identical to the baseline, and the applied-step logs contained no omissions or duplicates. Those are the reported outcomes for those cases; they do not, by themselves, describe every possible crash timing.
Does a bitwise match mean the results were merely close within a tolerance?
No. ‘Matched bitwise’ is stricter than a numerical closeness claim. The reported recovered parameters and moments had the same bit patterns as the baseline values in the comparisons.
If the state matched bitwise, why mention the step logs at all?

They report another aspect of recovery explicitly. The state comparison says what parameters and moments recovery produced; the logs say that, in the reported cases, applied steps were neither omitted nor duplicated. Keeping both observations visible avoids reducing the result to just one kind of check.
Do the logs establish that every update happened in the correct order?

The stated log result is zero omissions or duplicates. It does not separately report an ordering comparison, so I would not add that as a claimed observation. The bitwise state match remains the reported comparison of the resulting parameters and moments.
Can we say there was no duplicate application in any of the 10,000 seeded crashes?

We can say the applied-step logs showed zero duplicates across the 10,000 seeded crashes. That is the precise reported finding. It should not be expanded into a claim about crash cases outside those observations.
What about missing steps?

The same logs showed zero omissions across the 10,000 seeded crashes. Alongside zero duplicates, that describes the reported applied-step record without assuming any unreported details about the recovery process.
Did the recovered moments ever differ while parameters still matched?
No such difference is reported. The result says recovered parameters and moments matched the baseline bitwise across the 10,000 seeded crashes.
Does this result tell us exactly how an in-flight copy was handled after each crash?

No. It reports the recovered states and applied-step logs, not a per-crash account of how copies and deltas were interpreted. We should not infer a particular internal sequence from the matching outcomes alone.
Does it tell us that the failure-free step-time overhead is within 10% of static sharding?
No. This evidence reports crash-recovery state comparisons and applied-step logs. It provides no failure-free step-time measurement or overhead comparison against static sharding.

Certification would need to cover the *whole Adam state represented by a copy*, not just whether copying finished. When you say ‘both moments,’ what needs to line up?

Would it be enough for all the labels to show the same step number?

Where do the step counters fit? Aren't the parameters and moments the important part?

The question explicitly includes step counters in what must be certified. A copied state cannot claim to represent one committed Adam step if its counters describe different progress from its parameters or moments. Certification has to account for them as part of the same state, rather than treating them as incidental metadata.
Does copy-on-write guarantee that these components came from one step?

Not by itself. Copy-on-write can preserve versions while copying proceeds, but the certification question remains: which version of each component does the proposed snapshot include, and do those versions collectively represent one committed step? Merely retaining earlier data does not answer that.
Must every component be physically copied at precisely the same instant?

The requirement is a logically coherent snapshot of one committed step, not necessarily simultaneous physical transfers. Components could be copied at different times only if the design can still establish that their contents correspond to that same committed step. No method for doing so is specified in this question.
Then what should a copy manifest actually certify?

At a conceptual level, it would need to identify a complete set of parameters, both moments, and step counters whose contents represent a single specified committed Adam step. That is stronger than certifying the existence of a manifest or the completion of transfers. The exact contents of a manifest and the certification procedure remain open.
Is identifying the step enough, or must the manifest also establish commitment?

It must distinguish a committed step from an in-flight one. A snapshot accurately identified with a step that had not committed would not meet the question's ‘one committed Adam step’ condition. Step identity and committed status therefore both need an unambiguous interpretation.
Could a commit watermark establish that status?

A commit watermark could be relevant to identifying committed progress. But the watermark would also need to be consistently related to *every component* of the copy. Knowing that a step committed does not by itself show that the copied parameters, both moments, and counters all reflect that step.
What if a snapshot has parameters at step 71, but both moments and the counters at step 70?

That snapshot would not represent one committed Adam step, even if all its components were present. A certificate for step 70 would misdescribe the parameters; a certificate for step 71 would misdescribe the moments and counters. Certification has to exclude that combination rather than choose a step label for it.
What if the parameters and moments agree, but the counters lag?

It still would not satisfy the stated condition that parameters, both moments, and step counters come from one committed step. Agreement among some components cannot substitute for agreement of the entire certified state.
Could certifying each component separately solve the problem?

Separate certificates might help identify what each component represents, but they would not alone certify the *combination*. The replacement would still need a sound way to conclude that the specific parameters, first moment, second moment, and counters it uses together all represent one committed step.
Does a quorum certificate automatically establish that combination?

No. A quorum certificate is only as meaningful as the statement being certified and the checks behind it. If it attests solely that a copy finished, it does not establish step coherence. The question is how to make certification cover the complete, mutually consistent Adam state and its committed-step identity.
After an owner crashes mid-reshard, what should a replacement be able to determine from the certification?

It should be able to determine whether an available copy is a complete snapshot of parameters, both moments, and step counters from one committed step. Is this the same question as preventing an update from being replayed twice?

Could we approach elastic Adam resharding by replaying gradients rather than transferring every intervening optimizer-state change?

A proposal is to replicate ordered gradient batches, periodically checkpoint immutable Adam tuples, and rebuild migrating shards by deterministic replay behind epoch-fenced step tokens. The checkpoint would provide a starting state, and replay would reconstruct subsequent optimizer progress in the intended order. This is a proposed design, not a demonstrated recovery or performance result.
Why replicate the gradient batches in order?

Replay needs an unambiguous sequence of inputs. Having the same batches available without knowing their order would not establish which Adam state should result after each step. Replicating the ordered batches is intended to preserve the sequence needed to rebuild a migrating shard deterministically.
Does replicating a gradient batch mean its optimizer step has already committed?

No. Availability of an input and commitment of its optimizer step are separate facts. The proposal’s epoch-fenced step tokens would need to help recovery distinguish steps it may count from inputs that were available but should not become an extra update. The proposal does not yet define a complete commitment rule.
What is an immutable Adam tuple in this proposal?

It is a checkpointed optimizer-state unit that cannot be changed in place after it is recorded. To support rebuilding Adam state, it would have to capture a coherent starting point for the relevant parameters and moments, along with whatever step state replay requires. The proposal names immutable Adam tuples but does not specify their exact fields or serialization.
Why checkpoint those tuples periodically rather than replaying from the beginning?

A periodic checkpoint supplies a more recent starting point for replay. Conceptually, recovery could start from that immutable state and replay the subsequent ordered gradient batches instead of reconstructing all prior progress. The proposal does not set a checkpoint interval or claim a particular replay cost.
Does ‘immutable’ alone guarantee that a checkpoint is internally consistent?

No. Immutability prevents a recorded tuple from changing afterward; it does not, by itself, establish that every part of the tuple came from the same committed Adam step. The proposal would still need a sound way to identify the checkpoint’s step and ensure that its contents represent one coherent state.
What does it mean to rebuild a migrating shard?

Rather than assuming a copied shard is already at the required optimizer step, the proposed approach reconstructs the state needed under the changing shard assignment. It starts from an immutable Adam checkpoint and deterministically replays the ordered gradient batches relevant to the progression being rebuilt. The exact partitioning of those batches among migrating shards is not specified.
Would replay necessarily produce the same parameters and both Adam moments?

That is the intended result, but it is conditional on a coherent checkpoint, the correct ordered inputs, and genuinely deterministic replay of the intended steps. The proposal does not demonstrate that those conditions hold. Recovery still has to match the parameters and moments of uninterrupted deterministic execution after any single worker crash during resharding.
What are the epoch-fenced step tokens meant to control?

They are meant to associate an optimizer step with the appropriate shard-assignment epoch and keep work from another epoch from being accepted as the same authorized step. In this proposal, replay occurs behind those tokens so rebuilding a shard does not silently mix ownership contexts or count an update twice. The token format and enforcement procedure are not specified.
Is an epoch-fenced step token the same as a gradient batch ID?

Not necessarily. An ordered gradient batch identifies replay input, while an epoch-fenced step token is proposed to govern how a logical optimizer step is recognized under a shard-assignment epoch. The proposal does not define either identifier’s representation or say that the two can be treated interchangeably.
Suppose the same replicated gradient batch is seen twice during recovery. Should Adam run it twice?

Not if both appearances correspond to one logical committed step. That would duplicate an update and could change both parameters and moments. The proposed step tokens would need to make the intended step identity and its eligibility for replay unambiguous, even if its input is available from more than one place.
Could we simply replay every gradient batch after the most recent checkpoint?

Not solely because it is present after the checkpoint. Some available inputs might belong to steps that were not committed when the owner crashed. Recovery needs to know which steps belong to the intended progression and count each of those once. The proposal does not yet provide the full rule for deciding that boundary.
How does the epoch matter if the gradient order is already known?

Gradient order describes optimizer progress; the epoch distinguishes the shard-assignment context in which work is authorized. During elastic resharding, those contexts can change without making the ordered inputs themselves sufficient to determine which assignment may apply a step. Fencing is proposed to preserve that distinction.
If a worker crashes while a shard is migrating, what would recovery conceptually use?

It would need an appropriate immutable Adam tuple as a starting point, the replicated ordered gradient batches needed beyond that point, and an unambiguous interpretation of the epoch-fenced step tokens. It could then rebuild the migrating shard by deterministic replay of the intended steps. This is a conceptual account of the proposal, not a specified crash protocol or a claim that all required information is always available.
Would this require copying live parameters and moments while replay runs?

The proposal does not prescribe how live state is copied or whether particular transfers overlap with replay. Its named rebuilding mechanism is periodic immutable Adam checkpoints plus ordered gradient batches replayed behind epoch-fenced step tokens. Additional copying behavior should not be assumed from that description.
Is this proposal limited to crash recovery, or does it also concern normal resharding?

It concerns rebuilding migrating shards during elastic resharding, with replicated inputs and checkpoints also intended to make rebuilding possible after a crash. It must preserve the same optimizer-step progression in either case. The proposal does not describe a separate normal-reshard protocol.
Does deterministic replay mean results will match bitwise?

The recovery target is to match uninterrupted deterministic execution for parameters and moments. Calling replay deterministic expresses the intended reconstruction method, but the proposal alone does not establish bitwise matching or specify a test of it. The starting tuple, input order, and counted steps all have to agree with the reference execution.
What failure mode would an inconsistent checkpoint cause?

If the starting tuple combined state from different optimizer steps, replaying a correctly ordered sequence afterward would still begin from the wrong Adam state. Immutability would preserve that inconsistency rather than fix it. A coherent checkpoint is therefore necessary to the proposed rebuilding approach.
And what if the checkpoint is coherent but a batch is missing from the replicated sequence?

Then replay might not reconstruct the intended progression. Replication is proposed to make the ordered inputs available, but the proposal does not specify an availability guarantee or show that every required batch survives any single worker crash during resharding.
Would periodic checkpointing and batch replication automatically meet the step-time overhead limit?

No. Both can add failure-free work, and the proposal provides no step-time measurement for this approach. It would still need to limit failure-free step-time overhead to 10% versus static sharding with identical hardware and workloads.
Is recovery speed what that 10% limit measures?

No. The 10% requirement concerns failure-free step time. The proposal’s checkpoint frequency and replay length could matter to recovery behavior, but no recovery-time threshold is specified in that requirement.
Can we say that replay behind fenced tokens has already solved duplicate updates?

Not yet. It is the proposed means of preventing a logical step from being accepted under the wrong epoch or applied again during reconstruction. Whether the token rules actually provide that protection, including at a crash during resharding, remains to be established.
What is the proposal in one sentence, without presenting its outcomes as proven?

Replicate ordered gradient batches, periodically checkpoint immutable Adam tuples, and use deterministic replay behind epoch-fenced step tokens to rebuild migrating shards, while leaving recovery correctness and failure-free overhead to be established for this approach.
What is the plan for evaluating the gradient-log replay approach?

Implement gradient-log replay and epoch-fenced commits, then test crash recovery against deterministic Adam and benchmark step overhead against static sharding. The recovery test should address whether parameters and moments match uninterrupted deterministic execution after any single worker crash during resharding, without mixed steps or duplicate updates. The performance comparison should assess the 10% failure-free step-time overhead limit using identical hardware and workloads. This is a plan, not a report of results.
Why implement both replay and epoch-fenced commits before testing recovery?

They address different parts of the intended behavior.
